CHIEF COMPLAINT
Worsening headaches and evaluation of newly diagnosed pituitary lesion.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Mr. Bruce Ward is a 52-year-old male referred by Dr. Henry Howard for neurosurgical consultation regarding a pituitary lesion incidentally discovered during workup for worsening headaches. The patient initially presented to his primary care provider on 3/1/21 complaining of progressive headaches over the past three months. Headaches began approximately three months ago with gradual onset, initially 3/10 in severity and now 6/10. He describes the pain as a dull, nagging ache located behind both eyes, worse in the morning, lasting a few hours at a time with no identifiable alleviating or aggravating factors. The patient denies radiation of pain. He reports recent episodes of bumping into door frames but denies explicit awareness of visual changes. He denies fever, rash, neck stiffness, numbness, tingling, syncope, nausea, or vomiting. Eyes were checked in the fall with no reported concerns at that time. He tried acetaminophen several times without relief and discontinued it.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Denies fever, rash, neck stiffness, numbness, tingling, syncope, nausea, vomiting, or reported change in vision or balance.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Unremarkable. No chronic medical conditions.

MEDICATIONS
No current medications. Trial of acetaminophen for headaches without benefit.

ALLERGIES
Not documented.

FAMILY HISTORY
Patient is adopted with no known family history of medical illness.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Patient works as a computer programmer. Married for 25 years. Recently purchased a home. Denies alcohol use, tobacco use, and recreational drug use, never having used any of these substances.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: Alert and oriented to time, place, and person. Affect appropriate, speech fluent.
Neurological: Cranial nerves grossly intact. Visual acuity normal. Eye movements normal. Pupils equal and reactive to light. Visual field testing reveals bitemporal hemianopia. Color vision normal. No focal motor or sensory deficits in upper or lower extremities.

RESULTS
Laboratory studies from 3/3/21: CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, coagulation studies, and CRP all within normal limits. Pituitary hormone profile demonstrates low TSH; all other hormone levels normal.
Imaging: MRI brain with contrast from 3/4/21 reveals a well-defined pituitary lesion with elevation and compression of the optic chiasm. Ventricles normal in size. No other abnormalities noted.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Pituitary adenoma, benign-appearing, with optic chiasmal compression causing bitemporal hemianopia and headaches. Patient is symptomatic with clinical and radiographical evidence of optic chiasmal compression. Surgical intervention via transsphenoidal approach is indicated for excision and decompression of the pituitary fossa. Pathological examination of resected adenoma will be performed. Patient counseled on surgical risks including anesthesia complications (myocardial infarction, stroke, death), surgical complications (infection, further surgery needed, spinal fluid leak, meningitis, prolonged hospitalization, seizure, stroke, permanent neurological deficit, death). Pre-operative visual field testing ordered for baseline comparison. Referral placed to ophthalmology for comprehensive eye examination and formal visual field mapping prior to or shortly after surgery. Surgery scheduled through surgical scheduler. Patient to follow up post-operatively for vision assessment and recovery.
